Making a repository public cannot really be undone. Once it is visible, its whole history can be cloned, forked, cached and indexed, along with its issues, pull requests and every CI log. So Harness² Workbench went public in stages, and each stage had a checklist. This is that checklist, with what each step found.

1. Nothing in the history that should not be there

A secret deleted in the latest commit is still in the history. So the scans covered every commit, not the working tree:

  • Secrets. gitleaks over the full history, with a release binary whose checksum was verified against the published one before use. It scanned 180 commits and found nothing. The count did not match the 181 commits that change files, and the difference turned out to be one commit that only replaced a PNG screenshot, which gitleaks skips. If a scanner's count does not match yours, find out why before you trust the result.
  • Personal data. A search of every line ever added, in every commit, for home-directory paths, machine names, internal hostnames, private network addresses and the names of other private projects. The only hits were the generic private ranges used in a configuration example and a test.
  • Identities. Every commit records an author and a committer, with an email address. The repository's local Git configuration used the GitHub no-reply address from the first commit, and a check of every author and committer identity in the history showed only no-reply addresses: mine, Dependabot's and GitHub's. That includes merges made in GitHub's web interface, which take whatever email setting the account has, so that check is worth repeating after them.
  • Screenshots. The project was renamed that morning, before its first push (another project had the first name). Seven documentation screenshots were older than the rename; each one was opened and checked for the old name. None showed it.
  • CI logs. A public repository's past Actions logs become public too. The workflows use no secrets beyond GitHub's own token, which is masked.

2. Credit

harness2 is Google Research's work, and the Workbench is unofficial. The README says so in its first lines, the project's description says "Not affiliated with Google", and NOTICE credits harness2 (Apache-2.0, Copyright 2026 Google LLC) for the parts of the domain code that were translated from it and for the harness2 output used as test fixtures.

3. A clean clone, not a working tree

A working tree contains files that exist only on your machine: build output, generated assets, an ignored configuration that a test quietly reads. So before the first push the whole gate ran from a literal git clone into an empty directory outside the repository: formatting, the documentation link checker, clippy for native and WebAssembly targets, every test, cargo-deny, the dependency cooldown, the web bundle and the end-to-end suite against real harness2. Before tagging the release it ran again from a fresh clone, with the release build and the licence file added.

4. Private first

The repository went to GitHub as a private repository, with only main pushed. That turned out to matter: the first CI runs failed four tests that had always passed locally, and Dependabot's first proposals broke the dependency policy in three different ways. Both stories have their own posts (flaky tests, Dependabot). All of it was fixed while the repository was still private.

5. Turning on what the governance files promise

A SECURITY.md that points to private vulnerability reporting is a broken promise until that feature is switched on. Each governance file was checked against the repository's settings:

PromiseSetting
SECURITY.md: report vulnerabilities privatelyprivate vulnerability reporting on
SUPPORT.md: ask questions in DiscussionsDiscussions on
The issue forms label new issues triagethe triage label created
"Security fixes skip the cooldown"Dependabot alerts and security updates on
No secrets in commitssecret scanning with push protection
CodeQL and Scorecard in security.ymlCODE_SCANNING_ENABLED set, after going public
CONTRIBUTING.md: changes need green CI and a reviewa ruleset on main

Code scanning is gated behind a repository variable because it needs a paid plan on a private repository; the variable was set the moment the repository became public, and the scans were started by hand.

The ruleset on main blocks force-pushes and deletion, and lets a pull request merge only when ten named checks have passed and a code owner has approved it. New commits dismiss earlier approvals. Each required check is bound to the GitHub Actions app, so a status reported by some other integration under the same name does not count. The code owner is me, so only my approval counts. Because GitHub does not let anyone approve their own pull request, the repository admin role can bypass the rule, and the docs say so. The bypass was tested by the next push.

6. Reading the first code scan honestly

The first CodeQL and Scorecard run raised 15 alerts: two "critical", seven "high", five "medium", one "low". Each one was read against the code before anything was dismissed:

  • Two "critical" alerts for a hard-coded cryptographic salt turned out to be a mock server's random-data generator: a non-cryptographic FNV hash whose stream-name parameter happened to be called salt. CodeQL reports any constant that reaches a parameter of that name. Renaming it to stream closed both, and the mock data is unchanged.
  • A test's failure message dumped a job's whole environment, which would include the test's fake secret value. It now names what leaked, never the value.
  • The mock server logged raw browser reports. They are now escaped so they cannot forge log lines. CodeQL does not count that escaping as a fix, so the alert came back and was dismissed with that reason.
  • Six alerts were dismissed, each with its reason written on the alert. A "secret written to a log" was the name of the environment variable that holds a secret, not its value. A session cookie flagged for missing Secure is Secure whenever the site is served over HTTPS, and must not be over plain HTTP or the browser would drop it. One was a test's own assertion message. Three Scorecard findings were deliberate decisions: the admin bypass, a base image built locally rather than pulled, and an "unmaintained" advisory for a compile-time crate.
  • Five Scorecard alerts stay open, because they are true: the repository is less than 90 days old, its history has no reviewed pull requests, static analysis has run on only a few commits, there is no fuzzing yet, and there is no OpenSSF best-practices badge. Dismissing them would make the dashboard green without making anything better.

7. Releasing

The code compiled into a binary carries other people's licences, and most of them require shipping the licence text. A cargo xtask licenses command now writes the licence texts of every crate compiled into the servers and the web UI, ten licences in all, with cargo-about, using the same allow-list as cargo-deny and skipping test and build dependencies. The release workflow puts that file in every archive, and the all-in-one image carries it. The runner image copies the uv binaries from uv's own image, which carries no licence file, so uv's licence texts are vendored from the pinned tag. Their Git blob hashes match the upstream files exactly.

The release itself is a workflow, not a laptop build. A binary built on a developer's machine embeds that machine's paths, and nobody else can verify how it was made. On a version tag the release workflow checks that the tag matches the workspace version, builds both Linux targets with the web UI embedded, adds the licence file, writes a CycloneDX SBOM and checksums, attaches GitHub build-provenance attestations, and opens a draft release. A person downloads one archive, checks its checksum and provenance, runs the binary and the demo, and only then publishes the draft. A published tag is never moved: a broken release gets a new patch version.

Version 0.1.0 went out that way on 24 October 2026. The checksums of both archives and the SBOM matched, GitHub's provenance record for the three files named the release workflow at the v0.1.0 tag, and the downloaded binary served the web UI and ran the demo to the same numbers the README shows.

The checklist, short

  1. Scan the whole history for secrets, and reconcile the scanner's count.
  2. Search every added line for personal and internal data.
  3. Check every author and committer identity, again after web merges.
  4. Open every image the repository ships.
  5. Credit upstream work in NOTICE and the README; ship third-party licences.
  6. Run the full gate from a literal clone outside the tree.
  7. Go private first, let CI and the bots run, fix what they find.
  8. Turn on every setting the governance files promise, and protect main.
  9. Read each code-scanning alert against the code; dismiss with reasons; keep the true ones open.
  10. Release from CI, as a draft that a person verifies before publishing.
